text: `--abstain-if` is checked only when the assertion fails. When it holds, the record is an unsure: exit 7, and `"abstain": true` in place of `"assert": false`.
`--mock FILE`, or `ONESIE_MOCK=FILE` in the environment, answers from a file instead of the API. The gate, the exit codes, every output mode, `--out` and `--resume` run as they do for real.

`--resume` with `--id` skips answered records and asks the rest, failed ones included. A finished run rewrites the file in input order and keeps answered ids the input no longer has, unless `--prune` drops them. A changed fingerprint refuses with exit 2. A record whose content changed but whose id did not keeps its old answer. Without `--id`, it carries on by line count. It does not ask a failed record again, apart from the `--stop-on-error` case below, so a skipped error line still counts as failed toward exit 6 and `--stats`, under `-i request` too. Either way, a skipped record keeps its stored `--assert` outcome, so it counts toward the exit code and `--stats` as if it were judged again.
Only a successful response is stored. An error, a timeout or a response onesie cannot use is asked again next time.

The answers file is `-o json` lines. A plain stream run can resume it, given the same questions, model, `-i`, `--map` and `--id`, with `-o json` and no gate or merge. Any other run is refused as changed.

A file whose fingerprint does not match this run exits 2, naming the cause, such as changed questions, model or flags, or a fingerprint a newer onesie wrote. To regenerate the file, run again without `--offline` and `--resume`. The model and provider are part of the match, so pin both with `-m` and `--provider`.
**Response caching.** `--cache` or `ONESIE_CACHE=1` answers a repeated request from disk, so a script run again and again pays once for each distinct question.

**Fail CI when a calibrated gate drifts.** Keep the answers file beside the labels, and a CI step checks the gate against it with `--offline`, which needs no key and costs nothing. Exit 1 means a requirement no longer holds, and exit 2 that the file no longer matches the questions, so regenerate it.

`--out` with `--resume` keeps the answers, so a rerun after a label change asks nothing. A change to the questions makes the file stale, and `--resume` then refuses it. Delete `answers.jsonl` and `answers.jsonl.onesie`, or drop `--resume`, to ask again. Once you pick your own cuts, edit `assert` and `abstain_if` in your copy of the file.
Check validates an expression against the plan it will run over, before any network call. An expression that passes cannot fail to evaluate on a successful record.
Cuts reads, for each question a gate names, the cut it compares that question's value against. Only ID.value < X or ID.value >= X gives one, and a single other use of ID.value takes it away.
Package cli assembles the onesie command tree. It sits outside package main so the tree can be built and exercised in tests without spawning a process.
The factory reads flags, which are parsed after this returns, so it closes over the pointer. Installing it only when absent keeps an injected factory winning.

Any other cache error in a run, such as a full disk or a home directory onesie cannot write, turns the cache off for the rest of that run with one warning on stderr, and the run carries on against the API.

If the atomic push is rejected, neither the branch nor the tag reached `origin`. Usually `main` moved on `origin`, or the tag already exists there. Back out the local release as above, pull, and run `make release` again with the next version if the tag was taken.

`--min-confidence` needs `--fallback`. Below the threshold `.decision` becomes the fallback text instead of the model's pick, and `.fallback` reads `low_confidence`, so a consumer routes on that field rather than trusting a low confidence guess. Above it `.decision` is the pick and `.fallback` is absent, which an assertion reads as the empty string. When the request fails, the record still carries `.decision` set to the fallback, with `.fallback` reading `error` and an `.error` beside it, and the exit code is the failure's. Under `-q` the record is not printed: a low confidence answer exits 1 and a confident one exits 0. In an assertion, `team.fallback == ""` holds only for a confident answer that arrived.

Timeouts in `internal/jev` are per attempt, not per call. With the default policy a call retries twice, so it can outlast the attempt timeout. Bound a whole call with a context deadline or `WithTotalTimeout`.

The live suite and `make skills-check` both hide `ONESIE_MOCK` from the onesie they run, so an exported mock file never turns a live run into a mock one or fails a dry run.

Under `--stop-on-assert`, a skipped false assertion ends the run where a fresh run would stop. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume by line count whose last line is an error line drops that line, asks its record again and carries on. A run stopped by `--stop-on-error` leaves exactly that, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it was written without `--stop-on-error`, so the resume stops there before any request, with the code a fresh run exited with, rebuilt from the line's kind and status. A csv or tsv row keeps only the message, so there it exits 2. Either way, pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. The same holds under `-i request`. With `--id` the failed record is asked again, and stops the run only if it fails again.
**Do** write semantic commit messages. Start with a type, then a colon, then what changed. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `test`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `build`, `ci`.

An expired entry is only a miss, and the Put after it overwrites it. Another run with a longer lifetime may still read it. A stored time in the future comes from a clock that cannot be trusted, so it is a miss too.
Put stores value, which must be JSON, under key. It writes a temporary file and renames it over the entry, so a reader sees the old entry or the new one and never half of one.
A run's lifetime decides what it reads, not what it deletes, so a shorter one never removes an entry other runs still read. Under NoAliasTTL the run reads no alias entry and deletes none.
Abort reports whether a failure ends the whole run rather than the one record. It is how an authentication failure stops a stream that would otherwise fail the same way on every line.
WithBackend replaces the OS keyring, so a test needs no real keychain.
WithOpen replaces how a Store opens the credential file and its directory.
WithCreateTemp replaces how a Store opens the temporary file it writes before the rename.
A developer's exported ONESIE_MOCK would otherwise turn the live suite into a mock run.
Opened on the first write, so a command rejected before it writes leaves the file, and the answers a resume needs, untouched.
The newest line wins, since a resume appends after what the file held before.
The file still points wherever it pointed before, so the new item would be an orphan.
Removed while the lock is still held, so no run can take a lock on the old file after this one lets go of it.
A fresh run under --stop-on-assert or --stop-on-error would have stopped at this record, so nothing after it is read.
Order matters. RetryAfterError embeds APIError, so the typed check precedes the sentinels it would otherwise match, and silentError comes last so a real error joined to one keeps its code.

The credential file is the last source, after the provider's environment variable. Every dry run returns before a client is built, so opening the file here is what makes it invisible to a run that needs no key.

A container with no HOME makes os.UserHomeDir fail, and setting ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR is how a user copes with that. Resolving the home directory before the variables were consulted would break every variable rule at once on exactly those machines.
`--api-key` was removed, since argv is visible to other processes. Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or run `onesie auth set`.
Named once. The wrap used to add a spelling of its own, so the user read the flag twice.
Now that nothing follows a bare `--assert`, this no longer trips the check.
onesie was called jev until the rename, so older scripts may still call `jev`.
Previously a failed record stopped the stream. It now prints an error line and the run exits 6.
The cache used to live under the config dir. It moved to `~/Library/Caches/onesie` so backup tools skip it.
`-o markdown` replaces the old `--markdown` flag, which is gone.
Retries were unbounded before, which made a dead server hang CI. The default is now two.
We no longer write the fingerprint inside the answers file. It sits beside it in `FILE.onesie`.
This was split out of internal/cli so the plan can be tested without cobra.
`calibrate` no longer needs `--id`, since it falls back to the line number.
Since v0.2.0 the key is read from the keychain before the credential file.
An earlier version compared ids as numbers, so `7` and `"7"` were two records. Ids now match by their text.
The `--threshold` flag was renamed from `--cut` to match the question file.
Before the refactor this retried forever on a 429.
This used to panic on an empty state. It now exits 2.
Kept for scripts written against 0.1, which read `.answer` instead of `.value`.
`onesie questions` replaces `onesie list`, which printed only the repository set.
The mock file format changed in 0.3: one object per line instead of a single array.
Switched from gojq's default encoder to our own, since the old one sorted keys.
The install script no longer asks for sudo.
`ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` was added so an alias's answers can expire sooner than a day.
Moved here from cmd/onesie when the tree became testable in process.
The cache is now keyed by the provider as well as the request body.
The option took a path until the filesystem was injected. It now takes a FileReader.
WithClock was renamed to WithNow when the stats line started reading it.
Returning the error here used to print it twice, once from cobra and once from Execute.
This check moved into CheckFlags from the print path.
Kept after the switch to gotestsum, so an older Makefile target still works.
The first version of the lock was a file created with O_EXCL, which a kill left behind.
No longer sorted by id, since the input order is what a reader expects.
Replaced the retry loop with a backoff that the clock controls.
